nameStory: The Blue Angelfish gets its name from its stunning blue coloration and the wing-like shape of its fins, which reminded early observers of celestial angels. The scientific name 'bermudensis' honors Bermuda, where this species was first scientifically described and where it remains common in tropical waters.
description: The Blue Angelfish is a spectacular tropical marine fish with a deep, compressed body and brilliant blue coloration. These striking fish can grow quite large for angelfish, reaching up to 15 inches in length. Their bodies are disc-shaped and laterally flattened, with long, flowing dorsal and anal fins that give them their angelic appearance. While typically found in warm tropical waters, they occasionally venture into New England waters during warmer months.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brilliant blue body with a smooth, almost metallic sheen that catches light beautifully - the blue appears to shimmer when the fish moves

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, disc-like body that's dramatically flattened from side to side, creating a thin profile when viewed head-on

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long, flowing dorsal and anal fins that extend backward like angel wings, with pointed tips that trail gracefully

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth positioned at the front of the snout, perfect for picking at coral and small prey

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large for an angelfish, reaching dinner-plate size when fully grown, making them unmistakable in New England waters

habitat: Blue Angelfish are extremely rare visitors to New England waters, occasionally spotted around rocky reefs and jetties during the warmest summer months when Gulf Stream currents bring tropical species north. They prefer areas with good water clarity and some vertical structure like pier pilings or rocky outcrops. Any sighting in New England waters would be considered exceptional and likely represents a fish carried north by warm currents.

seasonality.spring: Not typically present in New England waters during spring as water temperatures are still too cold for this tropical species.
seasonality.summer: The only season when Blue Angelfish might appear in New England, during the warmest water temperatures of late summer when tropical currents are strongest.
seasonality.fall: May linger into early fall if water temperatures remain warm, but will disappear as temperatures drop below tropical levels.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England waters during winter months due to cold temperatures that would be fatal to this tropical species.

funFact: Blue Angelfish can live for over 20 years and actually start life looking completely different - juveniles have bright yellow bodies with curved blue stripes that gradually transform into the solid blue adult coloration, like a living mood ring that changes permanently with age!
confusionNotes: In New England waters, Blue Angelfish are most likely to be confused with their close relative the Queen Angelfish, but Queen Angelfish have a distinctive yellow tail and body markings, while Blue Angelfish are uniformly blue. Remember: 'Blue through and through' for Blue Angelfish versus 'Queen wears a golden crown' for the yellow-marked Queen Angelfish.
contextualKnowledge: Blue Angelfish sightings in New England are so rare that they often make local diving and fishing news when spotted. These fish are far outside their normal range when found here, representing 'vagrants' carried north by warm ocean currents - a phenomenon that may become more common with changing ocean temperatures.
compareHints: Blue Angelfish can be distinguished from their closest relative, the Queen Angelfish, by their uniform blue coloration throughout the body and fins. Queen Angelfish display bright yellow on their tails and often have yellow markings on their bodies, while Blue Angelfish maintain their solid blue appearance. Both species share the same basic body shape and fin structure, but the color difference is unmistakable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Queen Angelfish is distinguished from its close relative, the Blue Angelfish, primarily by the prominent crown-like spot on its forehead.
